text: Regex injection via unescaped glob bracket-set: attacker-controlled `pattern` passed to the public entry point `zipp.Path.glob` (zipp/__init__.py:401, EntryPoint hop_distance=0) flows into `re.compile(prefix + tr.translate(pattern))` at zipp/__init__.py:407. Along the way, `Translator.replace` (zipp/glob.py:59-68) returns `match.group('set') or (re.escape(match.group(0))...)` — i.e. when `separate()`'s named group `(?P<set>[\[].*?[\]])` (zipp/glob.py:106) matches a bracket expression, the raw pattern substring is returned with `re.escape` BYPASSED and spliced verbatim into the compiled regex. Because the `.*?` in the `set` group stops at the FIRST `]`, a pattern whose class ends in a backslash-escaped bracket (e.g. `Path(zf).glob('[a\\]')`) injects an unterminated character class into the final regex `(?s:[a\])\Z`, changing the regex's structure and raising an uncaught `re.error` out of `glob()` (whose only documented/guarded error is the `ValueError` raised at line 403 for an empty pattern). Callers that validate only `ValueError` crash. Same flow reaches `rglob` (zipp/__init__.py:411-412) via `self.glob(f'**/{pattern}')`.

text: zipp.Path performs NO normalization or containment check on the in-archive path `at`. `Path.__init__` stores the caller's `at` verbatim (zipp/__init__.py:303 `self.at = at`) and `Path.joinpath` builds the next path with bare `posixpath.join(self.at, *other)` (line 424) before handing it to `resolve_dir`, which only does a name-set membership lookup and never rejects anything. Because `posixpath.join` discards all preceding components when a later component is absolute, `zipp.Path(zf, 'subdir/') / '/etc/passwd'` yields `at='/etc/passwd'`, silently escaping the subdirectory scope; `..` segments are likewise never normalized or rejected, so `at='../../x'` is accepted. The missing control is a normpath/isabs/containment check on joined member names. Impact is strongest in the write direction: `Path.open` forwards the unvalidated `at` straight to `self.root.open(self.at, zip_mode, pwd=pwd)` (line 328) with `zip_mode = mode[0]` (line 325), so mode 'w' lets a caller author archive entries literally named `../../evil`, i.e. zipp can be used to MINT zip-slip payloads that any ordinary extractor will then write outside the destination. Consumers that treat a zipp.Path as scoped to a subtree, or that use its names to drive extraction/authorization, lose that invariant.

text: `Translator.__init__` guards its separator input with a bare `assert` instead of a raised exception: `assert seps and set(seps) <= set(_default_seps), "Invalid separators"` at zipp/glob.py:24. This is the ONLY validation of `seps` in the package, and Python strips all assert statements under `-O` / PYTHONOPTIMIZE=1, so in an optimized interpreter the check vanishes entirely and `self.seps = seps` (line 25) accepts any value. The unvalidated `self.seps` is then interpolated into regex character classes used to build the glob matcher: `rf'[^{re.escape(self.seps)}]*'` (line 66), `rf'[{re.escape(self.seps)}]+'` (line 79, used as the re.split pattern at line 80), and `rf'[^{re.escape(self.seps)}]+'` (line 93, used as the re.sub pattern at line 94). The `re.escape` calls do block regex-metacharacter injection, so the residual impact is malformed/degenerate patterns rather than arbitrary regex — e.g. `seps=''` produces the character class `[^]*`. The missing control is a real (non-assert) input validation that survives optimization. Note zipp's own call site hardcodes `Translator(seps='/')` (zipp/__init__.py:406), so this is reachable only via third-party use of the Translator class.

zipp/glob.py:24 implements the Translator separator-validation protection as a bare `assert`: `assert seps and set(seps) <= set(_default_seps), "Invalid separators"`. Python strips all `assert` statements when run under `-O` / `PYTHONOPTIMIZE`, so in an optimized deployment this validation is silently disabled and `self.seps` is accepted unvalidated. This matters beyond hygiene because `self.seps` is the backing value for the `restrict_rglob` protection: at glob.py:79-82 `restrict_rglob` builds `seps_pattern = rf'[{re.escape(self.seps)}]+'` and does `segments = re.split(seps_pattern, pattern)` before checking `any('**' in segment and segment != '**' ...)`. If `seps` is an arbitrary string (e.g. 'x' or a string not containing '/'), the pattern is no longer split on real path separators, so the `** must appear alone in a path segment` guard no longer evaluates real segments and can be bypassed — the ReDoS protection is defeated by a build flag. The class docstring at glob.py:8-20 documents the AssertionError as the intended contract (`>>> Translator('xyz')` -> `AssertionError: Invalid separators`), confirming this assert IS the protection and not an internal sanity check.

text: The `restrict_rglob` protection at zipp/glob.py:70-82 is an incomplete fix for the glob ReDoS it was written to prevent: it only rejects `**` when mixed *inside* a segment (`'**' in segment and segment != '**'`), so a pattern made of repeated standalone `**` segments such as `**/**/**/**/**/**/x` passes validation and is then translated by `replace()` (glob.py:64) into the chained-wildcard regex `.*/.*/.*/.*/.*/.*/x`, which is compiled at zipp/__init__.py:407 (`matches = re.compile(prefix + tr.translate(pattern)).fullmatch`) and run against every entry name. Chained `.*` separated by literals is the classic catastrophic-backtracking shape, giving super-linear blowup on non-matching long filenames. The exposure is widened by `Path.rglob` (zipp/__init__.py:411-412) which itself prepends a `**/` segment: `return self.glob(f'**/{pattern}')`, so a caller-supplied `rglob('**/**/**/...')` compounds it. The regression tests that would catch exactly this are the `@pytest.mark.flaky`-suppressed ones in lead 1, and the scanner independently ranked this construction as its top dynamic_regex finding.

text: Pattern-amplification ReDoS: the regex COMPILED at zipp/__init__.py:407 (`re.compile(prefix + tr.translate(pattern))`) is assembled from the caller-supplied glob `pattern`, and Translator.replace (zipp/glob.py:59-68) expands every `*` into the unbounded quantifier `[^/]*` and every `**` segment into `.*`. A pattern with k stars therefore yields k independent unbounded quantifiers separated by literal text (e.g. glob `*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*z` -> regex `(?s:[^/]*a[^/]*a...[^/]*z)\Z`). That compiled object is then applied as `.fullmatch` to EVERY member name of the archive (`filter(matches, names)` at line 409, `names` built from `self.root.filelist` at line 408). On a non-matching name of length n, CPython's backtracking engine explores O(n^k) splits, so a short pattern (~40 chars) against ordinary archive names causes super-linear CPU blowup. The only input validation on the path is `if not pattern: raise ValueError` (line 402) and `restrict_rglob` (zipp/glob.py:70-82), which constrains only WHERE `**` may appear, never how many stars a pattern may contain. Re-derive by calling `zipp.Path(z).glob('*a'*20+'*z')` on an archive whose names are long and non-matching.
